original_question: Let (wn) be a complex sequence such that the weighted averages (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N wn ψ(n) converge for every generalized 2-step nilsequence ψ. Must it follow that for every system (X, X, µ, T, S) and f, g ∈ L∞(µ), the averages (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N wn T^n f · S^n g converge weakly in L2(µ)?
target_in_paper: Section 4.2, "Variant of Special Case of Problem 3"; more precisely, your draft is the bilinear (ℓ = 2) specialization of that weighted open problem, to be read together with §2.4.2 for the definition of generalized nilsequences and §1.2 for the ambient notion of system.
correct_elements: Your draft captures the right open problem family: a weighted nilsequence-testing hypothesis implying weak L2 convergence of weighted multiple ergodic averages. It also gets the right bilinear specialization, the right mode of convergence (weak convergence in L2, not norm convergence), the right class of test objects in the bilinear case (generalized 2-step nilsequences), and the right type of conclusion involving two commuting transformations T and S acting on bounded functions f and g.
missing_details: The paper’s official formulation is an open problem in §4.2, specifically the weighted "Variant of Special Case of Problem 3"; your draft should identify itself as the bilinear (ℓ = 2) case of that statement rather than as an isolated question.
The ambient dynamical object should be stated as a probability measure-preserving system (X, Sigma, μ, T, S) with T and S commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations.

The phrase "generalized 2-step nilsequence" should be made stand-alone: it means a uniform limit of basic sequences of the form ψ(n) = F(g^n x), where X = G/Γ is a 2-step nilmanifold, G is a 2-step nilpotent Lie group, Γ is a discrete cocompact subgroup, x ∈ X, g ∈ G, and F is Riemann-integrable on X.
The official weighted variant uses generalized nilsequences, not only basic generalized nilsequences.
The sequence (w_n) is merely complex-valued; no boundedness hypothesis is assumed in the open problem itself. The paper separately notes that the bounded-weight case is already solved.
The domain of the indices and the limiting process should be stated explicitly: n runs over N and the Cesàro averages are taken as N → ∞.
To be fully stand-alone, weak convergence in L2(μ) should be unpacked: for every h ∈ L2(μ), the scalar sequence ∫ h · A_N dμ must converge, where A_N = (1/N)∑_{n=1}^N w_n T^n f · S^n g.
refined_question: Let (w_n)_{n≥1} be a complex sequence such that, for every generalized 2-step nilsequence ψ : N → C — that is, for every uniform limit of basic sequences ψ(n) = F(g^n x), where X = G/Γ is a 2-step nilmanifold, G is a 2-step nilpotent Lie group, Γ is a discrete cocompact subgroup, x ∈ X, g ∈ G, and F is Riemann-integrable on X — the Cesàro averages (1/N)∑_{n=1}^N w_n ψ(n) converge as N → ∞. Must it then follow that for every probability measure-preserving system (X, Sigma, μ, T, S) with T and S commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations, and every f, g ∈ L∞(μ), the weighted bilinear ergodic averages A_N := (1/N)∑_{n=1}^N w_n T^n f · S^n g converge weakly in L2(μ), i.e. that ∫ h A_N dμ converges for every h ∈ L2(μ)?
justification: The draft is clearly targeting §4.2 rather than any introductory theorem-like statement: it is about a complex weight sequence (w_n), testing against generalized nilsequences, and deducing weak L2 convergence of weighted double ergodic averages. This matches the paper’s "Variant of Special Case of Problem 3". The paper’s nearby context supplies the needed hidden assumptions: §1.2 gives the framework of commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations and bounded observables, while §2.4.2 defines (generalized) nilsequences and their multivariable/basic variants. Your draft is already very close, but to be fully paper-faithful and stand-alone it should explicitly state the commutativity/invertibility of T and S, the precise meaning of generalized 2-step nilsequence, and the weak-L2 meaning of the conclusion. I did not give an alternate formulation because the paper only says the nearby unweighted version is "probably of equivalent difficulty"; it does not prove an equivalence.
